claims.claim: The VOTC's DSMs were significantly correlated with the behavioral model in EBa (mean r = 0.12, p(one-tailed)FDR = 0.02) but not in SCa (mean r = 0.06; p(one-tailed)FDR = 0.17).
claims.source: In contrast, the VOTC's DSMs were significantly correlated with the behavioral model in EBa (mean r = 0.12, p(one-tailed)FDR = 0.02) but not in SCa (mean r = 0.06; p(one-tailed)FDR = 0.17).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by representational similarity analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The VOTC's DSMs were not significantly correlated with the pitch model neither in EBa nor in SCa.
claims.source: Finally the VOTC's DSMs were not significantly correlated with the pitch model neither in EBa(mean r = –0.03; p(one-tailed)FDR = 0.49), nor in SCa(mean r = 0.03; p(one-tailed)FDR = 0.39);
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by representational similarity analysis.

claims.claim: A 2 Groups (EBa/SCa) X 2 Models (behavioral/pitch) ANOVA in VOTC revealed a significant main effect of Model (F(1,31)=11.37, p=0.002) and a significant interaction Group X Model (F(1,31)=4.03, p=0.05).
claims.source: In addition, a 2 Groups (EBa/SCa) X 2 Models (behavioral/pitch) ANOVA in VOTC revealed a significant main effect of Model (F(1,31)=11.37, p=0.002) and a significant interaction Group X Model (F(1,31)=4.03, p=0.05), whereas the main effect of Group (F(1,31)=2.38−4, p=0.98), was non-significant.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ANOVA on representational similarity analysis data.

claims.claim: The correlation between subjects' DSMs in the within group condition was significant in SCv (r = 0.42; pFDR <0.001) and EBa (r = 0.10; pFDR <0.001), but not in SCa (r = –.03; pFDR = 0.98).
claims.source: The permutation test revealed that the correlation between subjects' DSMs in the within group condition was significant in SCv (r = 0.42; pFDR <0.001) and EBa (r = 0.10; pFDR <0.001), whereas it was not significant in SCa (r = –.03; pFDR = 0.98).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by inter-subject correlation analysis shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The correlation between subjects' DSMs was significant in all the three between groups conditions (SCv-EBa: r = 0.17, pFDR <0.001; SCv-SCa: r = 0.04, pFDR = 0.002; EBa-SCa: r = 0.02; pFDR = 0.04).
claims.source: Moreover, the correlation between subjects' DSMs was significant in all the three between groups conditions (SCv-EBa: r = 0.17, pFDR <0.001; SCv-SCa: r = 0.04, pFDR = 0.002; EBa-SCa: r = 0.02; pFDR = 0.04).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by inter-subject correlation analysis shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The highest inter-subject correlation is the within SCv group condition, which was significantly higher compared to all the other five conditions.
claims.source: When we ranked the correlations values (Figure 7) we observed that the highest inter-subject correlation is the within SCv group condition, which was significantly higher compared to all the other five conditions.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by inter-subject correlation analysis shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Both the between groups SCv-EBa and the within group EBa correlations were significantly higher compared to the last 3 inter-subjects correlation's values (between SCv-SCa; between EBa-SCa; within SCa).
claims.source: Interestingly, both the between groups SCv-EBa and the within group EBa correlations were significantly higher compared to the last 3 inter-subjects correlation's values (between SCv-SCa; between EBa-SCa; within SCa).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by inter-subject correlation analysis shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The representational connectivity profile of VOTC with the rest of the brain is significantly correlated between all pairs of groups (SCv-EBa: mean r = 0.18, pFDR = 0.001; SCv-SCa: mean r = 0.14, pFDR <0.001; EBa-SCa: mean r = 0.16, pFDR <0.001).
claims.source: The permutation analysis highlighted that the representational connectivity profile of VOTC with the rest of the brain is significantly correlated between all pairs of groups (SCv-EBa: mean r = 0.18, pFDR = 0.001; SCv-SCa: mean r = 0.14, pFDR <0.001; EBa-SCa: mean r = 0.16, pFDR <0.001), and with no difference between groups' pairs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by representational connectivity analysis shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: In EVC, the permutation analysis revealed a significant correlation only between the representational connectivity profile of the two groups of sighted: SCv and SCa (mean r = 0.17, pFDR <0.001).
claims.source: In this case the permutation analysis revealed a significant correlation only between the representational connectivity profile of the two groups of sighted: SCv and SCa (mean r = 0.17, pFDR <0.001), whereas the correlation between the EBa was not significant neither with SCv (mean r = 0.06, pFDR = 0.12) nor with SCa (mean r = 0.06, pFDR = 0.11).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by representational connectivity analysis in EVC.

claims.claim: VOTC shows categorical responses to sounds in the sighted and the blind in a representational format partially similar to the one elicited by images of the same categories in sighted people.
claims.source: Our study goes beyond previous results in at least six significant ways. First, our results demonstrate that VOTC shows categorical responses to sounds in the sighted and the blind in a representational format partially similar to the one elicited by images of the same categories in sighted people (see Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple analyses including topographical maps and decoding analyses.

claims.claim: Blind people show higher decoding accuracies and higher inter-subject consistency in the representation of auditory categories.
claims.source: Second, we observed that blind people show higher decoding accuracies and higher inter-subject consistency in the representation of auditory categories, and that the representational structure of visual categories in sighted was significantly closer to the structure of the auditory categories in blind than in sighted group (see Figure 1B, Figure 3, Figure 4B, Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by decoding accuracy and inter-subject correlation analyses.

claims.claim: In absence of feed-forward visual input, VOTC increases its intrinsic representation of non-visual information.
claims.source: This points to the idea that in absence of feed-forward visual input, VOTC increases its intrinsic representation of non-visual information.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of higher decoding accuracies in blind compared to sighted for auditory categories.

claims.claim: VOTC shows similar large-scale representational connectivity profiles when processing images in sighted and sounds in sighted and blind people.
claims.source: Third, VOTC shows similar large-scale representational connectivity profiles when processing images in sighted and sounds in sighted and blind people (see Figure 8).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by representational connectivity analysis shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: The functional tuning of a region is determined by large-scale connectivity patterns with regions involved in similar coding strategies.
claims.source: This result provides strong support to the general hypothesis that the functional tuning of a region is determined by large-scale connectivity patterns with regions involved in similar coding strategies (Behrens and Sporns, 2012; Mahon and Caramazza, 2011; Passingham et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical work and by the representational connectivity results.

claims.claim: Categorical membership is the main factor that predicts the representational structure of sounds in VOTC in blind people, rather than lower-level acoustical attributes of sounds.
claims.source: By harnessing the opportunities provided by representational similarity analysis, we demonstrate that categorical membership is the main factor that predicts the representational structure of sounds in VOTC in blind people (see Figure 6), rather than lower-level acoustical attributes of sounds that are at least partially at the basis of category selectivity in the temporal cortex (Moerel et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by representational similarity analysis comparing brain DSMs with behavioral and acoustic models.

claims.claim: The between-groups Jaccard similarity analysis revealed a domain–by–modality interaction, with the big objects and places category showing a higher degree of similarity between the auditory and visual representations compared to the other categories.
claims.source: Fifth, we provided a qualitative exploration of the structure of the categorical representation in the VOTC. The between-groups Jaccard similarity analysis revealed a domain–by–modality interaction (see Figure 2C), with the big objects and places category showing an higher degree of similarity between the auditory and visual representations compared to the other categories.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Jaccard similarity analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Both the hierarchical clustering and the within-group Jaccard similarity analysis highlighted a domain-by-sensory experience interaction, with the animal category represented differently in blind compared to sighted subjects.
claims.source: In addition, both, the hierarchical clustering and the within-group Jaccard similarity analysis highlighted a domain-by-sensory experience interaction (see Figure 5 and Figure 2B), with the animal category represented differently in blind compared to sighted subjects (Bi et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by hierarchical clustering and Jaccard similarity analyses.

claims.claim: Categorical membership is encoded in the EVC of blind people only, using a representational format that does not relate neither to the acoustic nor to the categorical structure of the stimuli.
claims.source: Finally, our study discloses that categorical membership is encoded in the EVC of blind people only, using a representational format that does not relate neither to the acoustic nor to the categorical structure of our stimuli, suggesting different mechanisms of reorganization in this posterior occipital region.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by decoding and representational similarity analyses in EVC.

claims.claim: Regular visual properties specific to each category like retinotopic eccentricity biases, curvature or spatial frequencies could drive the development of categorical response in VOTC for visual information.
claims.source: It was suggested that regular visual properties specific to each category like retinotopic eccentricity biases (Gomez et al., 2019; Malach et al., 2002), curvature (Nasr et al., 2014) or spatial frequencies (Rajimehr et al., 2011) could drive the development of categorical response in VOTC for visual information (Andrews et al., 2010; Baldassi et al., 2013; Bracci et al., 2018; Rice et al., 2014; see Op de Beeck et al., 2019 for a recent review on the emergence of category selectivity in VOTC).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claims.claim: The parahippocampal place area (PPA) and the fusiform face area (FFA) receive dominant inputs from downstream regions of the visual system with differential selectivity for high vs low spatial frequencies and peripheral vs. foveal inputs, causing them to respond differentially to place and face stimuli.
claims.source: For instance, the parahippocampal place area (PPA) and the fusiform face area (FFA) receive dominant inputs from downstream regions of the visual system with differential selectivity for high vs low spatial frequencies and peripheral vs. foveal inputs, causing them to respond differentially to place and face stimuli (Levy et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claims.claim: A proto-eccentricity map is evident early in development.
claims.source: For instance, a proto-eccentricity map is evident early in development (Arcaro and Livingstone, 2017) and monkeys trained early in life to discriminate different categories varying in their curvilinearity/rectilinearity develop distinct and consistent functional clusters for these categories (Srihasam et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claims.claim: Adults who had intensive visual experience with Pokémon early in life demonstrate distinct distributed cortical responses to this trained visual category with a systematic location supposed to be based on retinal eccentricity.
claims.source: Further, adults who had intensive visual experience with Pokémon early in life demonstrate distinct distributed cortical responses to this trained visual category with a systematic location supposed to be based on retinal eccentricity (Gomez et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Category membership independently of visual attributes is a key developmental factor that determines the consistent functional topography of the VOTC.
claims.source: Although our results by no means disprove the observations that inherent visual biases can influence the development of the functional topography of high-level vision (Gomez et al., 2019; Hasson et al., 2002; Nasr et al., 2014), our data however suggest that category membership independently of visual attributes is also a key developmental factor that determines the consistent functional topography of the VOTC.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing categorical responses in VOTC for sounds in blind and sighted.

claims.claim: VOTC responds to sounds using a similar distributed functional profile to the one found in response to vision, even in case of people that have never had visual experience.
claims.source: Our study demonstrates that VOTC responds to sounds using a similar distributed functional profile to the one found in response to vision, even in case of people that have never had visual experience.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data comparing blind and sighted groups.

claims.claim: Previous studies reported a residual categorical effect in VOTC when orthogonalizing category membership and visual features of visual stimuli.
claims.source: By orthogonalizing category membership and visual features of visual stimuli, previous studies reported a residual categorical effect in VOTC, highlighting how some of the variance in the neural data of VOTC might be explained by high-level categorical properties of the stimuli even when the contribution of the basic low-level features has been controlled for (Bracci and Op de Beeck, 2016; Kaiser et al., 2016; Proklova et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claims.claim: Category-selectivity has been observed in VOTC during semantic tasks when word stimuli were used.
claims.source: Category-selectivity has also been observed in VOTC during semantic tasks when word stimuli were used, suggesting an involvement of the occipito-temporal cortex in the retrieval of category-specific conceptual information (Handjaras et al., 2016; Borghesani et al., 2016; Peelen and Downing, 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claims.claim: Learning to associate semantic features and spatial contextual associations with novel objects influences VOTC representations.
claims.source: Moreover, previous research has shown that learning to associate semantic features (e.g., 'floats') and spatial contextual associations (e.g., 'found in gardens') with novel objects influences VOTC representations, such that objects with contextual connections exhibited higher pattern similarity after learning in association with a reduction in pattern information about the object's visual features (Clarke et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Visual imagery triggered by non-visual stimulation is unlikely to explain the processing of auditory information in the VOTC of sighted people.
claims.source: Even if we cannot fully exclude that the processing of auditory information in the VOTC of sighted people could be the by-product of the visual imagery triggered by the non-visual stimulation (Cichy et al., 2012; Kosslyn et al., 1995; Reddy et al., 2010; Slotnick et al., 2005; Stokes et al., 2009), we find it unlikely.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple lines of reasoning including experimental design choices and negative correlation results.

claims.claim: Two separate groups of sighted people were included, each performing the experiment in one modality only, to minimize the influence of having heard or seen the stimuli in the other modality.
claims.source: First, we purposely included two separate groups of sighted people, each one performing the experiment in one modality only, in order to minimize the influence of having heard or seen the stimuli in the other modality in the context of the experiment.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological design choice described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: A fast event-related design was used that restricted the time window to build a visual image of the actual sound.
claims.source: Also, we used a fast event-related design that restricted the time window to build a visual image of the actual sound since the next sound was presented quickly after (Logie, 1989).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological design choice described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: EVC does not discriminate the different sounds in the sighted group.
claims.source: Moreover, we would expect that visual imagery would also triggers information to be processed in posterior occipital regions (Kosslyn et al., 1999). Instead, we found that EVC does not discriminate the different sounds in the sighted group (Figure 3B and Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by decoding analysis results shown in Figure 3B and Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The decoding accuracy for the auditory categories in VOTC is significantly higher in the early blind compared to the sighted control group.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found that the decoding accuracy for the auditory categories in VOTC is significantly higher in the early blind compared to the sighted control group (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by decoding analysis results shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The correlation between the topographic distribution of categorical response observed in VOTC was stronger in blind versus sighted people.
claims.source: In addition, the correlation between the topographic distribution of categorical response observed in VOTC was stronger in blind versus sighted people (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by topographical selectivity map analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: The representational structure of visual categories in sighted was significantly closer to the structure of the auditory categories in blind than in sighted.
claims.source: Moreover, the representational structure of visual categories in sighted was significantly closer to the structure of the auditory categories in blind than in sighted (Figure 4A2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by representational similarity analysis shown in Figure 4A2.

claims.claim: The representation of the auditory stimuli in VOTC is more similar between blind than between sighted subjects.
claims.source: Finally, the representation of the auditory stimuli in VOTC is more similar between blind than between sighted subjects (Figure 7), showing an increased inter-subject stability of the representation in case of early visual deprivation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by inter-subject correlation analysis shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: A categorical organization similar to the one found in vision could emerge in VOTC in absence of visual experience.
claims.source: All together, these results not only demonstrate that a categorical organization similar to the one found in vision could emerge in VOTC in absence of visual experience, but also that such categorical response to sounds is actually enhanced and more stable in congenitally blind people.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing categorical responses in VOTC of blind individuals.

claims.claim: In absence of vision, the occipital cortex enhances its response to non-visual information processing.
claims.source: Several studies have shown that in absence of vision, the occipital cortex enhances its response to non-visual information processing (Collignon et al., 2012; Collignon et al., 2011; Sadato et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claims.claim: The expression of crossmodal plasticity, at least in VOTC, is constrained by the inherent categorical structure endowed in this region.
claims.source: In contrast with this view, our results demonstrate that the expression of crossmodal plasticity, at least in VOTC (see differences in EVC below), is constrained by the inherent categorical structure endowed in this region.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing similar categorical organization across groups.

claims.claim: VOTC reliably encodes sound categories in sighted and blind people using a representational structure and connectivity partially similar to the one found in vision.
claims.source: First, we highlighted remarkably similar functional profile of VOTC for visual and auditory stimuli in sighted and in early blind individuals (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by representational similarity analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: VOTC is encoding a similar categorical dimension of the stimuli across different inputs of presentation and different visual experiences.
claims.source: In addition, we showed that VOTC is encoding a similar categorical dimension of the stimuli across different inputs of presentation and different visual experiences (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by representational similarity analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The involvement of right dorsal occipital region for arithmetic processing in blind people relates to the intrinsic 'spatial' nature of these regions.
claims.source: In support of such idea, we recently demonstrated that the involvement of right dorsal occipital region for arithmetic processing in blind people actually relates to the intrinsic 'spatial' nature of these regions, a process involved in specific arithmetic computation (e.g. subtraction but not multiplication) (Crollen et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research by the authors.

claims.claim: The involvement of VOTC during 'language' may relate to the fact that some level of representation involved in language (e.g. semantic) can be intrinsically encoded in VOTC.
claims.source: Similarly, the involvement of VOTC during 'language' as observed in previous studies (Bedny et al., 2011; Burton et al., 2006; Kim et al., 2017; Lane et al., 2015; Röder et al., 2002) may relate to the fact that some level of representation involved in language (e.g. semantic) can be intrinsically encoded in VOTC as supported by the current results (Huth et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and inferred from current results.

claims.claim: VOTC regions have innate predispositions relevant to important categorical distinctions that cause category-selective patches to emerge regardless of sensory experience.
claims.source: In fact, we suggest that VOTC regions have innate predispositions relevant to important categorical distinctions that cause category-selective patches to emerge regardless of sensory experience.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results and represents a theoretical interpretation.

claims.claim: Items from a particular broad category (e.g. inanimate) are so diverse that they may not share systematic perceptual features and therefore a higher-level of representation, partially abstracted from vision, might prove important.
claims.source: One argument might be that items from a particular broad category (e.g. inanimate) are so diverse that they may not share systematic perceptual features and therefore a higher-level of representation, partially abstracted from vision, might prove important.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative argument provided to explain the results.

claims.claim: There is evidence in support of an extension of the intrinsic categorical organization of VOTC that is already partially independent from vision in sighted.
claims.source: Indeed, we gather evidence in support of an extension of the intrinsic categorical organization of VOTC that is already partially independent from vision in sighted.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing categorical responses to sounds in sighted individuals.

claims.claim: The crossmodal plasticity observed in early blind individuals may serve to maintain the functional homeostasis of occipital regions.
claims.source: An intriguing possibility raised by our results is that the crossmodal plasticity observed in early blind individuals may actually serve to maintain the functional homeostasis of occipital regions.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results.

claims.claim: The specific topographic location of a selective brain function is constrained by an innate profile of functional and structural connections with extrinsic brain regions.
claims.source: It is thought that the specific topographic location of a selective brain functions is constrained by an innate profile of functional and structural connections with extrinsic brain regions (Passingham et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous theoretical work.

claims.claim: The main fiber tracts are already present in full-term human neonates.
claims.source: Since the main fiber tracts are already present in full-term human neonates (Dubois et al., 2014; Dubois et al., 2016; Kennedy et al., 1999; Kostović and Judaš, 2010; Marín-Padilla, 2011; Takahashi et al., 2011), such initial connectome may at least partly drive the functional development of a specific area.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claims.claim: The visual word form area (VWFA) in VOTC shows robust and specific anatomical connectivity to EVC and to frontotemporal language networks and this connectivity fingerprint can predict the location of VWFA even before a child learn to read.
claims.source: Supporting this hypothesis, the visual word form area (VWFA) in VOTC (McCandliss et al., 2003) shows robust and specific anatomical connectivity to EVC and to frontotemporal language networks and this connectivity fingerprint can predict the location of VWFA even before a child learn to read (Saygin et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claims.claim: Anatomical connectivity profile can predict the location of the fusiform face area (FFA).
claims.source: Similarly, anatomical connectivity profile can predict the location of the fusiform face area (FFA) (Saygin et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claims.claim: FFA has a direct structural connection with the temporal voice area (TVA) in the superior temporal sulcus thought to support similar computations applied on faces and voices as well as their integration.
claims.source: In addition to intra-occipital connections, FFA has a direct structural connection with the temporal voice area (TVA) in the superior temporal sulcus (Benetti et al., 2018; Blank et al., 2011) thought to support similar computations applied on faces and voices as well as their integration (von Kriegstein et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claims.claim: The maintenance of selective structural connections between TVA and FFA explains the preferential recruitment of TVA for face processing in congenitally deaf people.
claims.source: Interestingly, recent studies suggested that the maintenance of those selective structural connections between TVA and FFA explains the preferential recruitment of TVA for face processing in congenitally deaf people (Benetti et al., 2018; Benetti et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claims.claim: The TVA-FFA connectivity may explain why voices preferentially map slightly more lateral to the mid-fusiform sulcus.
claims.source: This TVA-FFA connectivity may explain why voices preferentially map slightly more lateral to the mid-fusiform sulcus (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the connectivity hypothesis and the topographical mapping results.

claims.claim: Sounds of big objects or natural scenes preferentially recruit more mesial VOTC regions, overlapping with the parahippocampal place area, potentially due to the preserved pattern of structural connectivity of those regions in blind people.
claims.source: Similarly, sounds of big objects or natural scenes preferentially recruit more mesial VOTC regions (Figure 1B), overlapping with the parahippocampal place area, potentially due to the preserved pattern of structural connectivity of those regions in blind people (Wang et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by topographical mapping results and citation to previous research.

claims.claim: The existence of innate large-scale brain connections specific for each region supporting separate categorical domain may provide the structural scaffolding on which crossmodal inputs capitalize to reach VOTC in both sighted and blind people.
claims.source: The existence of these innate large-scale brain connections that are specific for each region supporting separate categorical domain may provide the structural scaffolding on which crossmodal inputs capitalize to reach VOTC in both sighted and blind people, potentially through feed-back connections.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the results.

claims.claim: The main white matter tracks including those involving occipital regions are not significantly different between blind and sighted individuals.
claims.source: Indeed, it has been shown that the main white matter tracks including those involving occipital regions are not significantly different between blind and sighted individuals (Shimony et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claims.claim: In early blind, the absence of competitive visual inputs from feed-forward inputs from EVC may trigger an enhanced weighting of feed-back inter-modal connections leading to an extension of selective categorical response to sounds in VOTC.
claims.source: In EB, the absence of competitive visual inputs typically coming from feed-forward inputs from EVC may actually trigger an enhanced weighting of those feed-back inter-modal connection leading to an extension of selective categorical response to sounds in VOTC, as observed in the current study.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the results.

claims.claim: The results provide crucial support for the 'biased connectivity' hypothesis.
claims.source: Our results provide crucial support for this 'biased connectivity' hypothesis (Hannagan et al., 2015; Mahon and Caramazza, 2011) showing that VOTC subregions are part of a large-scale functional network representing categorical information in a format that is at least partially independent from the modality of the stimuli presentation and from the visual experience.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental results and citations to previous theoretical work.

claims.claim: Intrinsic characteristics of objects belonging to different categories might drive different representations in the VOTC of the blind.
claims.source: Previous studies already suggested that intrinsic characteristics of objects belonging to different categories might drive different representations in the VOTC of the blind (Bi et al., 2016; Büchel, 2003; Wang et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claims.claim: In the early blind group, the number of voxels selective for animals is reduced compared to the other categories.
claims.source: We found that in the early blind group the number of voxels selective for animals is reduced compared to the other categories (see Figure 2A), suggesting that the animal category is under represented in the VOTC of early blind.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by voxel count analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The hierarchical clustering analyses highlight a reduced animate/inanimate division in the EBa group, with the animal and the humans categories not clustering together and the animals being represented more like tools or big objects.
claims.source: Our hierarchical clustering analyses (see Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1) also highlight a reduced animate/inanimate division in the EBa group, with the animal and the humans categories not clustering together and the animals being represented more like tools or big objects in the EBa.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Blind people normally learn the peculiar shape of each animal touching static miniature models of them.
claims.source: Blind people, instead, do normally learn the peculiar shape of each animal touching static miniature models of them.
claims.evidence: This is a statement based on general knowledge about how blind people learn about animals.

claims.claim: When blind people hear the sounds of animals without seeing them, they might combine these sounds with the rest of the environmental sounds.
claims.source: Moreover, when blind people hear the sounds of these animals without seeing them, they might combine these sounds with the rest of the environmental sounds, and this is indeed what we see in the behavioral ratings, in which only blind subjects cluster together animals and big environmental sounds.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the behavioral rating results.

claims.claim: The modality of presentation and/or the visual experience do affect the qualitative structure of the categorical representation in VOTC, and this effect is stronger for some categories (i.e. animals) compared to others (i.e. inanimate).
claims.source: These results therefore reveal that the modality of presentation and/or the visual experience do affect the qualitative structure of the categorical representation in VOTC, and this effect is stronger for some categories (i.e. animals) compared to others (i.e. inanimate).
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing differences in categorical representation across groups and categories.

claims.claim: Sound categories could be decoded in the EVC of EB but not of the SC.
claims.source: A different profile emerged from EVC. First, sound categories could be decoded in the EVC of EB (Figure 3B) but not of the SC.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by decoding analysis results shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The representational structure of EVC for sounds correlated to the one found in vision only in EB.
claims.source: In addition, the representational structure of EVC for sounds correlated to the one found in vision only in EB (Figure 4A2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by representational similarity analysis shown in Figure 4A2.

claims.claim: Neither the categorical membership nor the acoustic attributes of sounds correlated with the representational structure found in the EVC of EB.
claims.source: However, neither the categorical membership nor the acoustic attributes of sounds correlated with the representational structure found in the EVC of EB (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by representational similarity analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The posterior part of the occipital cortex in EB is the region that distances itself the most from the native computation it typically implements.
claims.source: A possible explanation for this result is that the posterior part of the occipital cortex in EB is the region that distances itself the most from the native computation it typically implements (Bi et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and represents an interpretation of the results.

claims.claim: Because EVC has a native computation that does not easily transfer to another sensory modality (i.e. low-level vision), it may rewire itself for distant functions.
claims.source: Because this area has a native computation that does not easily transfer to another sensory modality (i.e. low-level vision), it may therefore rewire itself for distant functions (Bedny, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citation to previous theoretical work.

claims.claim: Some studies reported an involvement of EVC in high-level linguistic or memory tasks.
claims.source: Some studies, for instance reported an involvement of EVC in high-level linguistic or memory tasks (Van Ackeren et al., 2018; Amedi et al., 2003; Bedny et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claims.claim: The categorical membership of sounds does not explain the representational structure of EVC in the current study.
claims.source: However, as demonstrated here, the categorical membership of sounds, which may be a proxy for semantic representation, does not explain the representational structure of EVC in our study.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the representational similarity analysis results.

claims.claim: Early visual deprivation is associated with significant changes in the structure of the brain itself, particularly within the occipital cortex.
claims.source: This is particularly relevant when comparing blind and sighted subjects given that blindness is associated with significant changes in the structure of the brain itself, particularly within the occipital cortex (Dormal et al., 2016; Jiang et al., 2009; Pan et al., 2007; Park et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claims.claim: Thirty-four participants completed the auditory version of the fMRI study: 17 early blinds and 17 sighted controls.
claims.source: Thirty-four participants completed the auditory version of the fMRI study: 17 early blinds (EBa; 10F) and 17 sighted controls (SCa; 6F).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claims.claim: An additional group of 16 sighted participants performed the visual version of the fMRI experiment.
claims.source: An additional group of 16 sighted participants (SCv; 8F) performed the visual version of the fMRI experiment.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claims.claim: All the blind participants lost sight at birth or before 4 years of age and all of them reported not having visual memories and never used vision functionally.
claims.source: All the blind participants lost sight at birth or before 4 years of age and all of them reported not having visual memories and never used vision functionally (see Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the blind participants' characteristics.

claims.claim: The three groups were age and gender matched.
claims.source: The three groups were age (range 20–67 years, mean ± SD: 33.29 ± 10.24 for EBa subjects, respectively 23–63, 34.12 ± 8.69 for SCa subjects, and 23–51, 30.88 ± 7.24 for SCv subjects) and gender (χ2 (2,50)=1.92, p=0.38) matched.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the study participants and matching procedure.

claims.claim: Sounds and images were used instead of words because the authors wanted to access and model the bottom-up cascade of sensory processing starting from the low-level sensory processing up to the more conceptual level.
claims.source: We decided to use sounds and images, instead of words, because we wanted to access and model the bottom-up cascade of sensory processing starting from the low-level sensory processing up to the more conceptual level.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological decision explained by the authors.

claims.claim: The final acoustic stimulus set included 24 sounds from 8 different categories that could be reduced to 4 superordinate categories.
claims.source: The final acoustic stimulus set included 24 sounds from 8 different categories (human vocalization, human non-vocalization, birds, mammals, tools, graspable objects, environmental scenes, big mechanical objects) that could be reduced to 4 superordinate categories (human, animals, manipulable objects, big objects/places) (see Figure 1 and Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the stimulus set used in the study.

claims.claim: Binary MVP-classification using SVM classifier was used to distinguish between two categories at a time.
claims.source: We performed a binary MVP-classification (using SVM - support vector machine classifier) to look at the ability of each ROI to distinguish between two categories at time.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the analysis method used.

claims.claim: With eight categories, there are 28 possible pairs, resulting in 28 binary MVP-classification tests in each ROI.
claims.source: With eight categories we can have 28 possible pairs, resulting in 28 binary MVP-classification tests in each ROI.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the analysis approach.

claims.claim: Binary MVP-classification was used as dissimilarity index to build neural DSMs.
claims.source: We used the binary MVP-classification as dissimilarity index to build neural DSMs (Carlson et al., 2013; Cichy and Pantazis, 2017; Cichy et al., 2013; Dobs et al., 2019; Haxby et al., 2014; Haxby et al., 2011; O'Toole et al., 2005; Pereira et al., 2009; Proklova et al., 2019) for each group, in order to compare the functional profile of the ROIs between the three groups.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the analysis method with citations to previous studies using similar approaches.

claims.claim: Binary MVP-classification was preferred over other dissimilarity measures because two experimental conditions that do not drive a response appear very dissimilar when using correlation-based measures but are indistinguishable when using decoding approaches due to cross-validation.
claims.source: We preferred to use binary MVP-classification as dissimilarity index to build neural DSMs rather than other types of dissimilarity measures (e.g. Pearson correlation, Euclidean distance, Spearman correlation) since two experimental conditions that do not drive a response and therefore have uncorrelated patterns (noise only, r ≈ 0) appear very dissimilar (1 – r ≈ 1). When using a decoding approach instead, due to the intrinsic cross-validation steps, we would find that the two conditions that don't drive responses are indistinguishable, despite their substantial correlation distance (Walther et al., 2016) since the noise is independent between the training and testing partitions, therefore cross-validated estimates of the distance do not grow with increasing noise.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological justification with citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Pitch was selected as the low-level auditory feature because it is distinctly represented in the auditory cortex and may create low-level bias of auditory category selective responses in the temporal cortex.
claims.source: Pitch corresponds to the perceived frequency content of a stimulus. We selected this specific low-level auditory feature for two reasons. First, previous studies showed that this physical property of the sounds is distinctly represented in the auditory cortex and may create some low-level bias of auditory category selective responses in the temporal cortex (Giordano et al., 2013; Leaver and Rauschecker, 2010; Moerel et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological justification with citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Among alternative auditory RDMs based on separate acoustic features, the pitch model correlated most with brain RDM extracted from the temporal cortex in the SCa group.
claims.source: Second, we confirmed with our own SCa group that, among alternative auditory RDMs based on separate acoustic features (e.g. Harmonicity on noise ratio, Spectral centroid), the pitch model correlated most with brain RDM extracted from the temporal cortex. This provided strong support that this model was maximally efficient in capturing the encoding of sounds based on acoustic features in auditory cortical regions (see Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

results.result: VOTC reliably encodes sound categories in both sighted and early blind individuals using a representational structure partially similar to visual categorical responses. The auditory selectivity maps in blind subjects partially matched visual maps in sighted controls (r=0.19, p<0.001), and decoding accuracy was significantly above chance in VOTC for both groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C14, C15, C30, C31, C34, C54, C68, and C83 collectively demonstrate through topographical mapping, correlation analyses, and decoding accuracy that VOTC encodes sound categories in both blind and sighted individuals with partial similarity to visual responses. The statistical evidence from multiple complementary analyses (topographical maps, decoding, RSA) converges to support this conclusion.

results.result: Sound categories are more reliably encoded in blind compared to sighted individuals, with higher decoding accuracies (EBa: 57% vs SCa: 54% in VOTC, p<0.046), stronger topographical correlations with visual maps, and greater inter-subject consistency (r=0.10 in EBa vs r=-0.03 in SCa).
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C32, C55, C76-C80 provide converging evidence from multiple analyses (decoding accuracy, topographical correlations, inter-subject consistency) that blind individuals show enhanced and more stable categorical responses to sounds in VOTC compared to sighted controls. The statistical comparisons are appropriately conducted and significant.

results.result: VOTC in blind individuals represents categorical membership of sounds rather than acoustic features. The VOTC DSM correlated significantly with the behavioral categorical model (r=0.12, p=0.02) but not with the pitch model (r=-0.03, p=0.49) in early blind participants.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C45, C46, C59, and C84 demonstrate through representational similarity analysis that VOTC in blind encodes categorical rather than acoustic information. The partial correlation approach appropriately controls for shared variance between models, and the significant correlation with behavioral but not pitch models supports the categorical interpretation.

results.result: VOTC shows similar large-scale representational connectivity profiles across all three groups (SCv-EBa: r=0.18, SCv-SCa: r=0.14, EBa-SCa: r=0.16, all p<0.001), supporting the hypothesis that functional tuning is determined by connectivity patterns with regions involved in similar coding strategies.
results.evaluation: Claims C57, C52, C58, and C102 demonstrate through representational connectivity analysis that VOTC maintains similar connectivity profiles regardless of modality or visual experience. The significant correlations across all group pairs with no significant differences between them provide strong support for the biased connectivity hypothesis.

results.result: A domain-by-modality interaction was observed, with the big objects and places category showing higher topographical similarity between auditory and visual representations (Jaccard similarity significantly higher, p<0.001) compared to other categories.
results.evaluation: Claims C60, C25, and C24 demonstrate through Jaccard similarity analysis that different categories show varying degrees of cross-modal similarity, with big objects/places showing the highest consistency. The statistical evidence from repeated measures ANOVA and post-hoc tests supports this domain-by-modality interaction.

results.result: A domain-by-sensory experience interaction was observed for the animal category, which showed reduced representation in blind compared to sighted individuals. In blind, animals clustered with non-living categories rather than with humans, and showed reduced voxel counts (p=0.02 vs SCv) and lower Jaccard similarity (p<0.01).
results.evaluation: Claims C61, C22, C23, C27, C29, C104, C105, C107, and C108 provide converging evidence from multiple analyses (hierarchical clustering, Jaccard similarity, voxel counts) that the animal category is represented differently in blind compared to sighted individuals. The statistical evidence is robust across multiple complementary methods.

results.result: Categorical membership is encoded in EVC of blind people only (decoding accuracy 55%, p<0.001), but this representation does not correlate with either categorical (r=0.004, p=0.47) or acoustic models (r=-0.08, p=0.94), suggesting different mechanisms of reorganization in this posterior region.
results.evaluation: Claims C62, C109, C110, C111, and C115 demonstrate that EVC in blind shows above-chance decoding but lacks correlation with both categorical and acoustic models. This pattern is distinct from VOTC and suggests a different form of reorganization, though the specific computational nature remains unclear.

results.result: Visual imagery is unlikely to explain categorical responses to sounds in VOTC of sighted individuals, based on experimental design (separate groups, fast event-related design) and the absence of sound discrimination in EVC of sighted controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C75 provide multiple lines of evidence against the visual imagery hypothesis: methodological controls (separate groups, fast presentation), lack of EVC activation in sighted during auditory tasks, and negative correlation with visual models. While not definitive, the converging evidence makes visual imagery an unlikely primary explanation.

results.result: In sighted individuals viewing visual stimuli, EVC DSM correlated with the Hmax-C1 low-level visual model (r=0.13, p=0.002) but not behavioral model (r=0.03, p=0.11), while VOTC DSM correlated with behavioral model (r=0.34, p<0.001) but not Hmax-C1 (r=-0.07, p=0.991).
results.evaluation: Claims C42 and C43 demonstrate the expected hierarchical organization in visual processing, with EVC representing low-level features and VOTC representing categorical information. The partial correlation approach appropriately controls for shared variance, and the pattern supports the validity of the analytical approach.

results.result: In both EBa and SCa groups, EVC DSMs did not correlate significantly with either behavioral or pitch models.
results.evaluation: Claim C44 reports non-significant correlations in EVC for both auditory groups with both models. The statistics are clearly reported with appropriate corrections. This negative result is important for understanding the differential reorganization of EVC versus VOTC.

results.result: The correlation between blind-auditory and sighted-auditory topographical maps (r=0.06) was significantly lower than correlations involving visual maps (SCv-EBa: r=0.19, p=0.0003; SCv-SCa: r=0.14, p=0.0004), but the correlation between EBa and SCv was not significantly different from SCa and SCv (p=0.233).
results.evaluation: Claims C16, C17, and C35 report statistical comparisons of correlation values between different group pairs. The permutation-based statistical approach is appropriate for non-independent data, and the pattern suggests that blind-auditory responses are more similar to visual responses than sighted-auditory responses are.

results.result: Within-group Jaccard similarity analysis revealed significant consistency in topographical maps for each category in each group (all p<0.001), with a significant main effect of Category (F(3,138)=18.369, p<0.001) and Group×Category interaction (F(6,138)=4.9, p<0.001).
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C21 report within-group consistency analyses using Jaccard similarity. The statistical approach (one-sample t-tests, repeated measures ANOVA) is appropriate, and the results demonstrate that categorical representations are consistent within groups but show category-specific and group-specific patterns.

results.result: Category-specific differences in voxel counts were observed within groups: in SCv, fewer voxels were selective for humans compared to other categories; in SCa, more voxels were selective for big objects/places compared to manipulable objects.
results.evaluation: Claims C26 and C28 report within-group differences in voxel counts across categories. The statistical tests are appropriate (paired t-tests with FDR correction), though some comparisons show marginal significance (p=0.08). These findings suggest category-specific differences in representation extent.

results.result: In EVC, only the correlation between SCv and EBa DSMs was significantly positive (r=0.19, p=0.0002), while correlations involving SCa were negative or non-significant.
results.evaluation: Claim C33 reports RSA results in EVC showing selective similarity between visual responses in sighted and auditory responses in blind. The permutation-based statistics are appropriate, and this pattern contrasts with the more widespread similarities observed in VOTC.

results.result: Hierarchical clustering analysis in VOTC revealed different categorical structures between groups: SCv showed living/non-living distinction at 2 clusters, while EBa showed human/non-human distinction with animals clustering with non-living categories.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C40 describe qualitative differences in hierarchical clustering patterns between groups. While this is a descriptive rather than inferential analysis, it provides important insights into the structure of categorical representations and complements the quantitative analyses.

results.result: Behavioral dissimilarity matrices were highly correlated across all three groups (SCa/EBa: r=0.85, SCa/SCv: r=0.95, EBa/SCv: r=0.89, all p<0.001), indicating similar categorical perception strategies.
results.evaluation: Claim C41 demonstrates that participants across all groups perceived categorical similarities in a consistent manner. This is important for validating the behavioral model used in RSA and shows that differences in brain representations are not driven by differences in categorical perception.

results.result: A 2×2 ANOVA (Group×Model) in VOTC revealed a significant main effect of Model (F(1,31)=11.37, p=0.002) and Group×Model interaction (F(1,31)=4.03, p=0.05), with behavioral model correlating more strongly than pitch model, particularly in EBa.
results.evaluation: Claim C47 reports ANOVA results comparing model fits across groups. The statistical approach is appropriate for comparing the relative strength of behavioral versus acoustic models, and the interaction suggests that the preference for categorical over acoustic representation is stronger in blind individuals.

results.result: Inter-subject correlation analysis revealed highest consistency within SCv (r=0.42, p<0.001), followed by between SCv-EBa (r=0.17, p<0.001) and within EBa (r=0.10, p<0.001), with lowest consistency in SCa (r=-0.03, p=0.98).
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C51 demonstrate differential inter-subject consistency across groups and conditions. The permutation-based statistics are appropriate, and the pattern suggests that visual responses are most consistent, blind-auditory responses are moderately consistent, and sighted-auditory responses are least consistent.

results.result: In EVC, representational connectivity profiles were significantly correlated only between the two sighted groups (SCv-SCa: r=0.17, p<0.001), with no significant correlations involving EBa.
results.evaluation: Claim C53 shows that EVC connectivity patterns differ between blind and sighted individuals, contrasting with the similarity observed in VOTC. This supports the interpretation that EVC undergoes more extensive reorganization in blindness compared to VOTC.

results.result: The authors propose that category membership independently of visual attributes is a key developmental factor determining VOTC topography, and that VOTC has innate predispositions for categorical distinctions that emerge regardless of sensory experience.
results.evaluation: Claims C67, C87, and C89 represent theoretical interpretations that go beyond the data. While the findings are consistent with this interpretation (categorical responses in blind, partial similarity across modalities), alternative explanations (e.g., learned associations, semantic mediation) cannot be definitively ruled out. The claims about 'innate predispositions' and 'key developmental factors' require developmental or genetic evidence not provided in this cross-sectional study.

results.result: The authors conclude that in absence of visual input, VOTC increases its intrinsic representation of non-visual information, and that crossmodal plasticity in VOTC is constrained by inherent categorical structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C56, C80, and C82 represent interpretations of the enhanced responses in blind individuals. While the data show stronger and more consistent responses in blind (C2, C55), the mechanism ('increases intrinsic representation' vs. reduced competition from visual inputs, enhanced attention, etc.) is not directly tested. The claim about 'constraint by inherent categorical structure' is an interpretation rather than a demonstrated mechanism.

results.result: The authors propose that crossmodal plasticity may serve to maintain functional homeostasis, and that innate connectivity patterns provide structural scaffolding for crossmodal inputs through enhanced weighting of feedback connections in absence of visual input.
results.evaluation: Claims C90, C99, and C101 are speculative mechanistic proposals not directly tested in this study. While consistent with the data (preserved topography, similar connectivity), these claims about homeostasis, feedback connections, and enhanced weighting require direct measurement of connectivity, developmental trajectories, or causal manipulations not provided here.

results.result: The authors suggest that blind people learn about animals through touching miniature models and may combine animal sounds with environmental sounds, explaining the different representation of animals in blind individuals.
results.evaluation: Claims C106 and C107 propose experiential explanations for the different animal representation in blind individuals. While C107 is supported by behavioral clustering data, C106 is an assumption about blind individuals' experience that is not empirically verified in this study. Individual differences in animal exposure and learning modalities are not assessed.

results.result: The authors propose that EVC in blind 'distances itself from native computation' and 'rewires for distant functions' because low-level vision does not transfer to other modalities.
results.evaluation: Claims C112 and C113 represent speculative interpretations of the EVC findings. While the data show that EVC in blind encodes categories without correlation to categorical or acoustic models (C111), the specific claim about 'rewiring for distant functions' is not demonstrated. The nature of the computation in reorganized EVC remains unclear, and alternative explanations (e.g., different acoustic features, task-related processes) are not ruled out.

results.result: The authors argue that items within broad categories are so diverse they may not share systematic perceptual features, necessitating higher-level representation partially abstracted from vision.
results.evaluation: Claim C88 is a speculative argument about why categorical representation might be important. This is not empirically tested in the study - the diversity of perceptual features within categories and the necessity of abstracted representations are assumed rather than demonstrated.

results.result: The study included 17 early blind participants (lost sight before age 4, no visual memories), 17 sighted controls for auditory experiment, and 16 sighted controls for visual experiment, with groups matched for age and gender.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C120 describe the participant characteristics and matching. The groups are appropriately matched for age and gender, and the blind participants meet standard criteria for early blindness. The separate sighted groups for each modality is a strength of the design.

results.result: The study used non-linguistic sensory stimuli (24 sounds from 8 categories) to investigate bottom-up perceptual processing from low-level sensory to conceptual levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C121 and C122 describe the rationale for stimulus selection and the final stimulus set. The choice of sensory rather than linguistic stimuli is well-justified for investigating sensory processing, and the stimulus set is well-characterized with appropriate validation (recognition >80%, representativeness ratings).

results.result: Binary SVM classification was used as the dissimilarity index for building neural DSMs because it avoids the problem of noise-driven dissimilarity that affects correlation-based measures when conditions do not drive responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C126 describe and justify the analytical approach. The choice of decoding-based dissimilarity over correlation-based measures is well-justified given the expectation of noisy responses in 'visual' regions to auditory stimuli. The methodological reasoning is sound and supported by appropriate citations.

results.result: Pitch was selected as the low-level auditory model because it is distinctly represented in auditory cortex and correlated most strongly with temporal cortex representations among tested acoustic features in the SCa group.
results.evaluation: Claims C127 and C128 justify the selection of pitch as the acoustic model through both theoretical reasoning (citations to prior work) and empirical validation (comparison of multiple acoustic features in Figure 6-supplement 1). This validation strengthens confidence that pitch is an appropriate low-level acoustic model.

results.result: The introduction reviews prior literature on occipital cortex organization, showing that while some theories emphasize visual feature-based proto-organization, other studies demonstrate preserved categorical organization in blind individuals.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C13 accurately summarize prior literature on occipital cortex plasticity and organization. These are appropriately cited background claims that establish the theoretical context and motivation for the current study. The citations appear accurate based on the described findings.

results.result: The discussion reviews extensive prior literature on visual feature biases in VOTC development, category-selective responses, connectivity-based organization, and structural brain differences in blindness.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C66, C69-C71, C81, C91-C96, C100, C103, C114, and C116 accurately cite and summarize relevant prior literature. These background claims provide context for interpreting the current findings and are appropriately referenced. The integration of prior work supports the theoretical framework.

results.result: The authors cite their own prior work showing that occipital reorganization in blind relates to intrinsic computational properties (spatial processing for arithmetic, semantic processing for language).
results.evaluation: Claims C85 and C86 reference prior work by the authors to support the interpretation that reorganized occipital cortex maintains computations related to its intrinsic properties. These are appropriately cited and used to support the current interpretation.

results.result: The authors propose that preserved connectivity patterns (TVA-FFA for voices, parahippocampal connections for places) may explain the topographical mapping of sound categories in VOTC.
results.evaluation: Claims C97 and C98 propose connectivity-based explanations for observed topographical patterns. While C98 cites supporting evidence for preserved connectivity in blind, C97 is more speculative. The current study does not directly measure these specific connections or test whether they predict the observed topography.
